newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Senate head slams BoF selection method.
newsitem.headline: French Senate head slams BoF selection method.

text.p: The chairman of the French Senate on Friday criticised the procedure taken to appoint two new members to the Bank of France's monetary policy council, adding to the political controversy surrounding the decision.

"By not choosing any of the candidates proposed by the leaders of the legislative chambers, the government has not respected the spirit of the 1993 law relative to the status of the Bank of France to ensure diversity and balance in recruiting CPM members or the practice respected since the initial appointments," Senate Chairman Rene Monory said in a statement.

The government on Friday appointed Pierre Guillen, former head of the employers' federation CNPF, and Jean-Rene Bernard, former deputy governor at property lender Credit Foncier, to the nine-member council.

The new appointees, replacing Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, were proposed by the Economic and Social Council (CES) and are said to be close allies of President Jacques Chirac and more flexible in terms of interest-rate policy.

The parliamentary chambers and CES each propose two candidates, but under traditional practice, the body that chose the outgoing members has the prerogative to name the replacements. The Senate and CES nominated the departing members.
Monory wanted to reappoint Boissonnat, viewed as an advocate of the central bank's strong franc policy and of European monetary union, and Pierre Achard.
Monory said he "regrets the conditions in which the two appointments for the Bank of France monetary policy council were carried out".
He said he would introduce legislation to ensure the prerogatives in choosing appointments.

Earlier the chairman of the finance commission of the National Assembly, the lower house, said he was concerned by the decision not to reappoint Boissonnat, given Boissonnat's strong advocacy of European monetary union.
The government moved quickly to quell speculation that its appointments heralded any shift in French monetary policy.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said the nominations did not signal a change in direction.
President Jacques Chirac called on the Bank of France "to conduct monetary policy in stability and continuity," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said.
The newspaper Le Monde said in an editorial on Friday that the appointments "confirms the executive's suspicions relating to independent institutions".

It said the government's move also highlighted some of the contradictions in its approach toward European monetary union. "Today (Chirac) has appointed to key posts people who are not true believers in monetary union," the afternoon newspaper said in its January 6 edition.

"The chief of state has effectively retained the candidates of (National Assembly leader Philippe) Seguin -- subtly passed onto (CES chairman Henri) Matteoli's list -- against those of Monory," it said. It added that Chirac's move risked baffling his German partners.
